pages.name: Quantum Dot · Colour by Size

pages.name: Strömgren Sphere

pages.name: Matter Stars
pages.blurb: Matter stars: every star we have ever observed. The Sun turns 4.26 million tonnes of mass into light every second.

pages.name: Antimatter Stars
pages.blurb: Antimatter stars: by CPT symmetry an antistar would shine exactly like a star. You could only tell them apart by the 511 keV and pion-decay gamma rays where it touches ordinary matter.

pages.name: Gravity Stars
pages.blurb: Gravity stars: the objects that are mostly gravity. Black holes are real. Gravastars and boson stars are hypothetical. Gravitational-wave sources are where we actually "see" them.

pages.name: Annihilation · E = mc²
pages.blurb: When matter meets antimatter, 100% of the rest mass becomes energy. One gram of each gives about 43 kilotons of TNT.

pages.name: Positronium & the 511 keV Line
pages.blurb: An electron and a positron briefly orbit each other as positronium, then annihilate into gamma rays of exactly m_e c² = 511 keV.

pages.name: The Galactic 511 keV Glow
pages.blurb: The Milky Way's centre glows at 511 keV: positrons annihilate there at about 10⁴³ per second, and their source is still a mystery.

pages.name: Baryon Asymmetry
pages.blurb: Why is there anything at all? For every ~1.6 billion photons there is about one baryon, and almost no antibaryons.

pages.name: Sakharov's Three Conditions
pages.blurb: Andrei Sakharov, 1967: to make more matter than antimatter, a universe needs three things.

pages.name: CP Violation · Kaons
pages.blurb: 1964: neutral kaons decayed in a way that broke CP symmetry, the first crack between matter and antimatter.

pages.name: CPT Symmetry
pages.blurb: Flip charge, mirror space and reverse time together, and physics stays the same. That is why an antistar would look exactly like a star.

pages.name: ALPHA · Antihydrogen Spectrum
pages.blurb: CERN's ALPHA experiment shone a 243 nm laser on trapped antihydrogen. The 1S–2S line matched hydrogen to about 2 parts in 10¹².

pages.name: ALPHA-g · Antimatter Falls Down
pages.blurb: 2023: ALPHA-g let antihydrogen fall. It fell down, at about 0.75 g with large errors, consistent with ordinary gravity.

pages.name: Antiprotons in Cosmic Rays
pages.blurb: Cosmic rays contain about 1 antiproton per 10,000 protons, made in collisions rather than in antistars.

pages.name: The Positron Excess
pages.blurb: PAMELA (2009) and AMS-02 found more high-energy positrons than expected, rising above ~10 GeV.

pages.name: AMS-02 Antihelium & Antistar Limits
pages.blurb: An antihelium nucleus would be hard to make by collisions, which is why AMS-02's handful of candidates attracted attention.

pages.name: Black Holes · Schwarzschild
pages.blurb: Schwarzschild found the first black-hole solution in 1916, in a WWI trench. A 10-solar-mass black hole is 59 km across.

pages.name: Gravastars
pages.blurb: A gravastar (Mazur and Mottola, 2001): a hypothetical shell of exotic matter around a de Sitter vacuum core, with no horizon and no singularity.

pages.name: Boson Stars
pages.blurb: A boson star is a hypothetical star made of a scalar field: a giant coherent wave held together by its own gravity.

pages.name: GW150914 · The First Chirp
pages.blurb: 14 Sept 2015: LIGO heard two black holes of 36 and 29 suns merge into one of 62. Three suns' worth of mass left as gravitational waves.

pages.name: LIGO · Measuring 10⁻¹⁸ m
pages.blurb: LIGO's 4 km arms change length by a thousandth of a proton's width. Gravity stars announce themselves this way.

pages.name: The Torus · Euler Characteristic 0
pages.blurb: A torus has V − E + F = 0: genus 1, one hole, the shape of Dave's toroid.

pages.name: The Flat Torus
pages.blurb: Glue the opposite edges of a square and you get a torus with zero curvature everywhere. Pac-Man and Asteroids are played on one.

pages.name: Torus Knots
pages.blurb: A (p,q) torus knot winds p times around one way and q times around the other. The trefoil is (2,3).

pages.name: Tokamak · Plasma Toroid
pages.blurb: A tokamak bottles a star in a toroid. ITER aims for 500 MW of fusion power from 50 MW of heating.

pages.name: Toroidal Fields Inside Stars
pages.blurb: Inside the Sun, differential rotation winds poloidal field lines into toroidal bands: the Ω-effect of the solar dynamo.

pages.name: Penning Traps · Holding Antimatter
pages.blurb: Antimatter is stored in Penning traps: a strong magnetic field plus electric end-caps. CERN's BASE kept antiprotons for over a year.

pages.name: The Ideal Toroid · Ampère
pages.blurb: Inside a wound toroid the field is B = μ₀NI/(2πr). Outside it is zero, which is why the toroid is the perfect magnetic bottle in textbooks.

pages.name: Matter × Antimatter × Gravity
pages.blurb: How Dave's three types would interact: matter and antimatter annihilate (100%), both fall into gravity stars (up to 5.7–42%), and matter stars burn by fusion (0.7%).

pages.name: FRB 20240304B · Farthest Fast Radio Burst

pages.name: SAPPHIRES · Protocluster at z = 8.47

pages.name: DESI · Is Dark Energy Weakening?
pages.blurb: DESI's second data release (March 2025) favours dark energy that evolves, w(a) = w₀ + wₐ(1 − a), over a constant Λ at 2.8–4.2σ depending on the supernova sample. That is a hint, not a 5σ discovery.

pages.name: Chiral Superconductor in Graphite

pages.name: p-Wave Magnetism · NiI₂
pages.blurb: A new kind of magnetism: in nickel iodide, spins form left- and right-handed spirals that are mirror images, and a small electric field flips one into the other.

pages.name: Magnonic Superradiant Phase Transition
pages.blurb: Rice University saw a superradiant phase transition predicted half a century ago, in a magnetic crystal of erbium, iron and oxygen: two spin systems lock into collective motion with no trigger.

pages.name: The Kakeya Conjecture in 3D
pages.blurb: Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl proved that any set containing a unit needle pointing in every direction must be fully three-dimensional (dimension 3), even though its volume can be zero.

pages.name: The Noperthedron · Not Rupert
pages.blurb: The first convex polyhedron proved not to have Rupert's property: no copy can pass through a straight tunnel in another copy. It has 90 vertices, 240 edges and 152 faces, rebuilt here from the authors' coordinates.

pages.name: Hilbert's Sixth · Particles → Fluid
pages.blurb: Deng, Hani and Ma derived the fluid equations from Newton's laws for hard-sphere particles, by way of Boltzmann's equation. It is a major case of Hilbert's 1900 sixth problem.

pages.name: Ochre · One Stop Codon

pages.name: Syn57 · Life on 57 Codons

pages.name: Mirror Life · A Warning

pages.name: Element 116 via Titanium-50 · The Road to 120

pages.name: Levinthal’s Paradox · 3²⁰⁰ vs a Millisecond
pages.blurb: A 100-residue chain has 200 backbone torsions. At 3 states each that is 3²⁰⁰ ≈ 2.7 × 10⁹⁵ shapes, so a blind search would outlast the universe by 10⁶⁵, yet small proteins fold in milliseconds or less.

pages.name: Anfinsen’s Dogma · The Sequence Knows
pages.blurb: Anfinsen unfolded ribonuclease A, scrambled its 4 disulfides, and watched it refold to full activity. The native fold is the free-energy minimum, written in the sequence. Random pairing of 8 cysteines gives 105 options, and only 1 is native.

pages.name: Energy Landscapes & Folding Funnels
pages.blurb: Folding is a descent on a rugged funnel: many high-entropy unfolded states at the rim, one low-energy native state at the bottom. The exact density of states of a 14-residue HP chain shows the funnel in numbers, with Z, P(native) and the heat-capacity peak.

pages.name: The HP Lattice · Fold It Yourself
pages.blurb: Dill’s HP model: residues are H (hydrophobic) or P (polar) on a lattice, and each non-bonded H–H contact scores −1. Fold the classic 20-mer benchmark by hand and let Dave’s I-13 VM count the energy and catch crossings from raw coordinates.

pages.name: Why Folding Is NP-Hard
pages.blurb: Finding the lowest-energy HP fold is NP-complete in 2D (Crescenzi et al. 1998) and in 3D (Berger & Leighton 1998). The number of chain shapes grows like 2.638ⁿ on the square lattice, so exact search hits a wall long before real protein sizes.

pages.name: Ramachandran Plot · φ and ψ
pages.blurb: Each residue’s backbone has two free torsions, φ (C–N–Cα–C) and ψ (N–Cα–C–N). The peptide bond ω is fixed near 180°. Atoms clash in most of the φ/ψ square, so helices and sheets sit in a few allowed islands. Click the plot to set φ and ψ, and the I-13 VM measures them back from the built atoms.

pages.name: α-Helix & β-Sheet · 3.6 per Turn
pages.blurb: Pauling’s α-helix has 3.6 residues per turn, a 1.5 Å rise and a 5.4 Å pitch, with each C=O bonded to the N–H four residues on. β-strands lie about 3.3 Å per residue and pair into sheets. The I-13 VM builds the helix with its own sine series.

pages.name: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS · Two-State Folding
pages.blurb: Proteins are only marginally stable, often 5–15 kcal/mol, the small difference of two huge terms ΔH and TΔS. With a heat-capacity change ΔC_p the stability curve bends down at both ends: heat and cold denaturation. Two-state kinetics give the chevron plot.

pages.name: Metropolis & Simulated Annealing
pages.blurb: Metropolis (1953) keeps a move that raises the energy by ΔE with probability e^(−ΔE/T). Annealing (Kirkpatrick 1983) lowers T slowly so the chain can escape traps. Here a 48-mer is annealed against a quench, with every acceptance table built by the I-13 VM.

pages.name: Femtoseconds vs Milliseconds · MD & Anton
pages.blurb: Molecular dynamics must step at about 2 fs to follow bond vibrations (a C–H stretch lasts 11 fs), but folding takes µs to s. That is 10⁹–10¹⁵ steps. D. E. Shaw’s Anton machines reached 85 and then 212 µs/day on the DHFR benchmark.

pages.name: AlphaFold2 & CASP14 · Solved and Unsolved
pages.blurb: At CASP14 (2020), AlphaFold2 reached a median domain GDT_TS of 92.4 and 0.96 Å backbone accuracy, against 2.8 Å for the next best method. It largely solved single-chain structure prediction, but not how proteins fold, how they move, or disorder.

pages.name: Misfolding · Prions & Amyloid
pages.blurb: Misfolded proteins can stack into amyloid, cross-β fibrils with strands 4.7 Å apart and sheets about 10 Å apart, linked to Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and prion disease. Growth is sigmoidal, and adding seed fibrils removes the lag.

pages.name: Nash Equilibrium · No Regrets
pages.blurb: A Nash equilibrium is a strategy for each player such that nobody gains by changing alone. Nash proved in 1950 that every finite game has one if mixing is allowed. Type any 2 × 2 game and the I-13 VM finds every equilibrium, pure and mixed.

pages.name: Prisoner’s Dilemma · Axelrod’s Tournaments
pages.blurb: In one round, defecting always pays more, yet two defectors do worse than two cooperators. Axelrod’s 1980 computer tournaments, with 14 entries and then 62, were both won by the simplest rule: TIT FOR TAT. Here 7 classic strategies replay a 200-move round-robin on the I-13 VM.

pages.name: Mixed Strategies & Minimax
pages.blurb: Some games have no stable pure choice: in Matching Pennies or a penalty kick, any pattern can be exploited. The answer is to randomise. Von Neumann’s 1928 minimax theorem says every zero-sum game has a value that both sides can guarantee, and the I-13 VM finds it.

pages.name: Hawk–Dove · Evolutionarily Stable Strategies
pages.blurb: Animals fighting over a resource of value V can escalate (Hawk) or display (Dove); escalating risks an injury costing C. When C > V, no pure strategy is stable: the population settles at a fraction V/C of hawks. Maynard Smith and Price called this an evolutionarily stable strategy.

pages.name: Coordination & Mechanism Design
pages.blurb: In a coordination game everyone wants to match, but there can be several equilibria: hunt the stag together, or each take a safe hare. Mechanism design runs the other way: choose the rules so selfish play gives the outcome you want. Vickrey’s second-price auction makes honest bidding optimal.

pages.name: Repeated Games & the Folk Theorem
pages.blurb: Play the Prisoner’s Dilemma again and again, and the future can discipline the present. If players value tomorrow enough (discount factor δ ≥ 1/2 here), grim trigger keeps cooperation going. The folk theorem says almost any fair-enough average payoff can be sustained.
pages.crumb: GAME THEORY · THE SHADOW OF THE FUTURE

pages.name: Bayesian Games & Signaling
pages.blurb: When players hold private information, they are of different types, and what they do can reveal their type. Harsanyi turned this into Bayesian games; Spence showed that costly education can signal productivity even when it teaches nothing. Both the separating and the pooling outcome can be equilibria.

pages.name: Punch-Out Tells · The Rose Triad as a Signaling Game
pages.blurb: Punch-Out opponents telegraph their attacks: a flash, a wind-up, a sound. Reading a tell is a signaling game, because the opponent can also feint. Here Dave’s rose triad (OBSERVE 0.3 s through the {{-2,0,3}} filter, RESPOND 0.2 s, SUB ID 0.1 s always watching .3.2) runs on the I-13 VM, frame by frame.

pages.name: Three Streams · Trust as Bayesian Updating
pages.blurb: Patricia hears three streams. LS Patricia learns and reacts, Toph centers and observes, RS probes warily, and each watches a different third of the screen (the t245 COOP views). Fusing them well is Bayesian: keep a Beta belief in each stream and weight its vote by log-odds. The I-13 VM does the updating.

pages.name: RED · BLUE · GREEN · Shapley Values
pages.blurb: Dave’s four-sapphon radial: RED (what happens to Patricia, and memory), BLUE (how to respond), GREEN (was it successful), with Patricia’s amethyst core making the final call. Treat the three as a coalition: how much of a good turn does each deserve? Shapley’s 1953 value answers that, and the I-13 VM computes it.

pages.name: The JIT Radial · ±1° per Turn as a Random Walk
pages.blurb: Dave’s Just-In-Time radial: a 360° ring whose needle moves +1° when a turn worked and −1° when it failed, with two tracks: what was tried and what happened, and what has happened and why. Mathematically, the needle is a random walk. The I-13 VM computes its exact distribution and the gambler’s-ruin odds.

pages.name: Star Polygons {n/k} · Schläfli
pages.blurb: Join every k-th of n points on a circle and you draw the star polygon {n/k}. If gcd(n, k) = 1 it is one stroke; otherwise it falls apart into a compound, like the hexagram {6/2} = two triangles. The I-13 VM computes the gcd and every vertex with its own sine series.

pages.name: The Four Kepler–Poinsot Stars
pages.blurb: There are exactly four regular star polyhedra. Kepler found the two stellated dodecahedra (1619), Poinsot added the great dodecahedron and great icosahedron (1809), and Cauchy proved there are no more (1813). All four are built here from the icosahedron’s and dodecahedron’s vertices, and the VM checks Euler and Cayley.

pages.name: Stella Octangula · Two Tetrahedra
pages.blurb: Extend the eight faces of an octahedron until they meet again and you get Kepler’s stella octangula: two interpenetrating tetrahedra, eight points, the only stellation of the octahedron. It fills exactly half of its cube. Slide the fold and watch the caps rise.

pages.name: Folded Paper Stars · Lucky Stars & Froebel
pages.blurb: Tie a paper strip in an overhand knot, flatten it, and the knot is a regular pentagon. Wrap the rest of the strip around it and pinch the edges, and it puffs into a lucky star. Four woven strips make a 16-pointed Froebel star. The I-13 VM computes the pentagon and the fold angles.

pages.name: Game Theory & Sapphons · Index
pages.blurb: Dave asked for game theory, his sapphons, and folded stars. Fifteen pages: seven on real game theory, four that read Patricia’s sapphon architecture as games, and four on star polygons, star polyhedra and paper stars. Every page boots his I-13 engine, checks its SHA-256 and computes on the VM.

pages.name: Kepler's Cubes
